sections.title: Walk the flowchart
sections.intro: It's Monday morning. You open a terminal to check on the cluster and `kubectl` isn't cooperating. Work out where the failure is before you touch anything.

questions.prompt: Before diagnosing anything, what's the most useful thing to notice about the failure?
options: Whether the same command worked yesterday
Which command you ran — some need more permissions
How long kubectl waited before it gave up
Whether any response came back at all, even a rejection
questions.explanation: Any HTTP response, even a 403, proves apiserver is alive, parsed your request, and made a decision. No response points at the process, the network path, or TLS. That one distinction cuts the problem in half before you read a single log. (Asking teammates is a good off-path check, but it comes later.)

questions.prompt: You see this. Which side of the fork are you on?
questions.snippet:
$ kubectl get nodes
The connection to the server 10.0.1.10:6443 was refused - did you specify the right host or port?
options: No response — the TCP connection itself was refused
A response — apiserver rejected the request
RBAC — you can't list nodes at cluster scope
TLS — the server's certificate was rejected
questions.explanation: "Refused" happens at the TCP layer, before HTTP or TLS. Nothing about your identity or permissions has been evaluated yet.

questions.prompt: What does "connection refused" specifically tell you that a timeout wouldn't?
options: The serving certificate has expired
A firewall is silently dropping your packets
The host answered, but nothing is listening on 6443
DNS resolved the server name to the wrong IP
questions.explanation: A refusal is an active answer: the kernel on that host sent back a reset. So the network path works. A timeout is silence, which points at firewalls and routing instead. Refused sends you to the process; timeout sends you to the network.

questions.prompt: kubectl can't help you, since it talks to the thing that's down. Where do you go next?
options: Restart every node so kubelet starts fresh
The node itself: `crictl ps -a`, `crictl logs`, the manifest
`kubectl get pods -n kube-system` with more verbosity
Regenerate your kubeconfig from scratch
questions.explanation: On kubeadm, apiserver is a static pod that kubelet runs straight from a manifest file, so you inspect it at the runtime level. A missing or broken manifest makes the process disappear. Rebuilding your kubeconfig can't fix a server that isn't running.

questions.prompt: The apiserver container keeps exiting. Its last log lines read like this. What's actually broken?
questions.snippet:
Error while dialing: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:2379: connect: connection refused
F1025 ... failed to connect to etcd
options: etcd — apiserver exits when it can't reach its storage
Your kubeconfig — it points at the wrong port
apiserver's binary — the image is corrupt
kube-proxy — it isn't routing to 2379
questions.explanation: A crashing apiserver is often a symptom, not the cause. apiserver won't start without etcd, so fixing apiserver's manifest would get you nowhere. Follow the logs to etcd (file 04).

questions.prompt: Different Monday. This time you see this, and the cluster is exactly one year old. What happened, and what do you NOT need to touch?
questions.snippet: Unable to connect to the server: x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid
options: The CA expired — regenerate it, then everything else
Leaf certs expired — renew them, leave the CA alone
Your laptop's clock drifted — resync it
RBAC rejected you — the binding expired
questions.explanation: The one-year anniversary is the classic giveaway. The TLS handshake fails before any HTTP happens, so this is still the no-response side of the fork. Replacing the CA would be far more disruptive than the problem calls for, because everything that trusts the CA would need to change. (A wrong clock can cause this error too, but the anniversary makes it unlikely here.)

questions.prompt: After renewing, `kubectl get nodes` now returns this. Is apiserver healthy?
questions.snippet: Error from server (Forbidden): nodes is forbidden: User "jdoe" cannot list resource "nodes" in API group "" at the cluster scope
options: Unclear — etcd needs checking before you can say
Yes — it identified you and made an RBAC decision
No — the renewed certs still aren't loaded
No — Forbidden means apiserver is failing
questions.explanation: A 403 is apiserver working correctly. It knows exactly who you are. `kubectl auth can-i list nodes` confirms it, and the fix is a RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding for the right principal, scoped no wider than needed.

questions.prompt: Before you declare a cluster-wide outage, which off-path check matters most?
options: Run `kubectl get componentstatuses`
Your current context — and try from a second machine
Restart kubelet on every control-plane node
Recreate the kube-system namespace
questions.explanation: The wrong context, a stale DNS entry, or a firewall rule that only blocks your IP all look exactly like a dead cluster from where you're sitting. Two seconds of checking avoids paging the whole team over your own laptop. (`componentstatuses` also goes through apiserver, so it can't work here either.)

sections.title: Read the signal
sections.intro: Each one stands alone. Place it on the fork, then name the likely cause.

questions.snippet: Unable to connect to the server: dial tcp 10.0.1.10:6443: i/o timeout
options: Your token — it expired mid-request
The certificate — the handshake stalled
The apiserver process — it crashed
The network path — firewall, security group, routing
questions.explanation: A crashed process on a reachable host usually produces a fast refusal. A timeout means your packets never got an answer, so look at the path: firewalls, security groups, routes, VPN. Test with `nc -vz 10.0.1.10 6443`.

questions.snippet: error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)
options: Network — the connection dropped midway
TLS — the handshake failed before HTTP
Authentication — apiserver can't tell who you are
Authorization — RBAC denied the action
questions.explanation: 401 means "I don't know who you are." 403 means "I know who you are, and no." A 401 is fixed in your kubeconfig credentials, not in RBAC. `kubectl auth whoami` helps when you aren't sure which identity is being sent.

questions.prompt: A response came back. Is this a "you" problem like 401/403?
questions.snippet: Error from server: etcdserver: request timed out
options: Yes — RBAC evaluation is too slow
No — apiserver is fine; its backend (etcd) is failing
No — the network to apiserver is flaky
Yes — your credentials timed out
questions.explanation: This is the branch the original flowchart skipped: a response that isn't a rejection of you. Network, TLS, and auth all worked. The failure is behind apiserver. Go to etcd.

questions.prompt: What's different about this error compared to "certificate has expired"?
questions.snippet: Unable to connect to the server: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority
options: Trust — your kubeconfig expects a different CA
Clock — the server's time is wrong
RBAC — the CA isn't bound to your user
Time — the cert expired, so renew it
questions.explanation: Expired is a time problem. Unknown authority is a trust problem. Renewing certs won't fix a kubeconfig that points at the wrong CA, so check `certificate-authority-data` and which cluster you're actually aimed at.

questions.prompt: In an HA cluster with three apiservers behind a load balancer, every kubectl call times out, but SSHing into each control-plane node shows apiserver running and healthy. Where's the problem?
options: All three apiservers — they're secretly broken
RBAC — the LB's identity was revoked
etcd — it's refusing the apiservers
The load balancer / VIP in front of them
questions.explanation: From the client, a dead LB and three dead apiservers look identical. Checking the backends directly is what separates them. Healthy backends behind a silent endpoint means the LB.

questions.prompt: Someone was editing `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` in place and kubectl started refusing connections. Why is in-place editing risky here?
options: Every edit also forces an etcd restart
kubelet acts on every save — a bad file kills the pod
The scheduler caches the old manifest
The file is read-only, so edits silently fail
questions.explanation: Static pods are driven entirely by files on disk. Prepare the new manifest elsewhere and move it in with one atomic step. And never leave backup copies in that directory, because kubelet will try to run those too.
